lines.s: # No commit-graph yet. A path-limited log has to compare trees commit by commit:
# Git reports statistics about changed-path filters through trace2. Without a file there are none:
# The file starts with the signature CGPH and a table of chunks:
# The same question again. One filter per commit was consulted:
# A path that few commits touch:
100bb99 schemas, gateway, ingest: add the tenant field in one change
00eae68 schemas: add the event types and their JSON schemas
printf '\nSee docs/runbooks for the on-call procedures.\n' >> README.md
git commit -q -am 'readme: point to the runbooks'
# A commit-graph is a snapshot. New commits are not in it until it is written again:
printf '\nSee docs/runbooks for the on-call procedures.\n' >> README.md
git commit -q -am 'readme: point to the runbooks'
# Maintenance adds a small file on top instead of rewriting the large one:
# A replacement object changes what the history is, so Git stops trusting the file:
# The switch that bypasses the file for one command:
GIT_TRACE2_PERF=1 git -c core.commitGraph=false log --oneline -- services/ranker 2>&1 >/dev/null | grep

beats.text: An evaluation team asks one question many times a day: which commits changed the scoring rubric? A commit is one saved snapshot of the whole project. The command is git log with a path. On their repository, with its long history, the answer takes twenty seconds each time.
beats.tele: An evaluation team asks one question many times a day: which commits changed the scoring rubric? A commit is one saved snapshot of the whole project. The command is `git log` with a path. On their repository, with its long history, the answer takes twenty seconds each time.

beats.text: The repository isn't broken. To answer, Git compares the tree of every commit with its parent's tree, one commit after another, to find the few that touched the path. A tree is a commit's listing of one directory. The fix isn't a smaller history. It's a file that lets Git dismiss most commits without looking at their trees. Keep those twenty seconds in mind. They come back.

beats.text: The commit-graph. In one sentence: it is a file that stores, for every commit, its parents, its root tree, its date and its distance from the roots of history, and optionally a compact summary of the paths it changed, so that history walks stop decompressing commit objects and stop comparing trees that didn't change.
beats.tele: The commit-graph. In one sentence: it is a file that stores, for every commit, its parents, its root tree, its date and its distance from the roots of history, and optionally a compact summary of the paths it changed, so that history walks stop decompressing commit objects and stop comparing trees that didn't change.

beats.text: Two things are stored, and they help different commands.
beats.tele: Two things are stored, and they help different commands.

beats.text: First, the graph with generation numbers. A commit's generation is larger than that of every ancestor.
beats.tele: First, the graph with generation numbers. A commit's generation is larger than that of every ancestor.

beats.text: A walk that asks "is A an ancestor of B" can stop as soon as it reaches commits whose generation is below A's, instead of walking to the root. This is what git merge-base, git branch --contains, git tag --contains and git log --graph gain from.
beats.tele: A walk that asks "is A an ancestor of B" can stop as soon as it reaches commits whose generation is below A's, instead of walking to the root. This is what `git merge-base`, `git branch --contains`, `git tag --contains` and `git log --graph` gain from.

beats.text: Second, changed-path Bloom filters, written with --changed-paths. For each commit, a small probabilistic set of the paths that differ from its first parent. Asked "did this commit touch services/ranker?", a filter answers "definitely not" or "maybe". Only the "maybe" commits need their trees compared. This is what git log with a path and git blame gain from.
beats.tele: Second, changed-path Bloom filters, written with `--changed-paths`. For each commit, a small probabilistic set of the paths that differ from its first parent. Asked "did this commit touch `services/ranker`?", a filter answers "definitely not" or "maybe". Only the "maybe" commits need their trees compared. This is what `git log` with a path and `git blame` gain from.

beats.text: Who writes the file? You can, with git commit-graph write --reachable --changed-paths. git gc writes one, and the setting is gc.writeCommitGraph, default true. The commit-graph maintenance task writes one incrementally. And fetch.writeCommitGraph does it after fetches. Filters are written only if you requested them once, or with commitGraph.changedPaths=true, which needs Git 2.52 or later.
beats.tele: Who writes the file? You can, with `git commit-graph write --reachable --changed-paths`. `git gc` writes one, and the setting is `gc.writeCommitGraph`, default true. The `commit-graph` maintenance task writes one incrementally. And `fetch.writeCommitGraph` does it after fetches. Filters are written only if you requested them once, or with `commitGraph.changedPaths=true`, which needs Git 2.52 or later.

beats.text: Failure modes. A stale file is slower, not wrong: Git notices commits that are missing from the file and reads those from the objects. A damaged file is another matter, and Lab 16.4 produces one. And Git stops using the file altogether in some repositories. The manual's caveat: "The existence of replace objects or commit grafts turns off reading or writing to the commit-graph." The same holds in a shallow repository.
beats.tele: Failure modes. A stale file is slower, not wrong: Git notices commits that are missing from the file and reads those from the objects. A damaged file is another matter, and Lab 16.4 produces one. And Git stops using the file altogether in some repositories. The manual's caveat: "The existence of replace objects or commit grafts turns off reading or writing to the commit-graph." The same holds in a shallow repository.

beats.text: The multi-pack-index. In one sentence: it's one sorted index over the objects of many packs, so that finding an object costs one lookup however many packs there are. A pack is one file that stores many objects, and each pack has its own .idx.
beats.tele: The multi-pack-index. In one sentence: it's one sorted index over the objects of many packs, so that finding an object costs one lookup however many packs there are. A pack is one file that stores many objects, and each pack has its own `.idx`.

beats.text: With N packs, a lookup may search N indexes. Geometric repacking, fetches and partial clones all produce many packs on purpose, so the cost has to be removed elsewhere: the file objects/pack/multi-pack-index maps every object ID to a pack and an offset. Git reads it when core.multiPackIndex is true, the default.
beats.tele: With N packs, a lookup may search N indexes. Geometric repacking, fetches and partial clones all produce many packs on purpose, so the cost has to be removed elsewhere: the file `objects/pack/multi-pack-index` maps every object ID to a pack and an offset. Git reads it when `core.multiPackIndex` is true, the default.

beats.text: Reachability bitmaps. In one sentence: a bitmap file stores, for selected commits, one bit per object in the pack saying whether that commit reaches it, so that a server can answer "which objects does this client need" without walking the graph. Serving a clone or fetch starts with enumerating objects: everything reachable from the wanted commits minus everything reachable from the ones the client has. With bitmaps that is a few bitwise operations, and stretches of the existing pack can be copied to the client verbatim.

With bitmaps that is a few bitwise operations, and stretches of the existing pack can be copied to the client verbatim.

beats.text: Why is this a server feature? The setting repack.writeBitmaps "defaults to true on bare repos, false otherwise". A bare repository has no working tree, and it's the kind a server holds. And scalar sets pack.useBitmaps=false on clients, with the reason that bitmaps "are optimized for server-side use, not client-side use".

And `scalar` sets `pack.useBitmaps=false` on clients, with the reason that bitmaps "are optimized for server-side use, not client-side use".

says: Written by default only in bare repositories: the kind a server holds

beats.text: The working tree. In one sentence: the untracked cache remembers which directories contained no untracked files, the file-system monitor tells Git which paths changed since the last command, and together they replace the scan of the working tree by a question.
beats.tele: The working tree. In one sentence: the untracked cache remembers which directories contained no untracked files, the file-system monitor tells Git which paths changed since the last command, and together they replace the scan of the working tree by a question.

beats.text: Recall the two kinds of work in git status: an lstat call per tracked file, and a walk of every directory in search of untracked files. The untracked cache, core.untrackedCache, attacks the second: the index records the modification time of each directory, and a directory whose time hasn't changed isn't read again.
beats.tele: Recall the two kinds of work in `git status`: an `lstat` call per tracked file, and a walk of every directory in search of untracked files. The untracked cache, `core.untrackedCache`, attacks the second: the index records the modification time of each directory, and a directory whose time hasn't changed isn't read again.

beats.text: Its default is keep, and feature.manyFiles=true and scalar switch it on. The file-system monitor, core.fsmonitor=true, attacks the first: a daemon, git fsmonitor--daemon, subscribes to the operating system's change notifications for one working tree, and git status calls lstat only on the paths it reports. The manual lists caveats: it doesn't know about submodules, and it refuses network-mounted repositories by default.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy for the commit-graph: a railway timetable printed from the day's train records. Asking the timetable is faster than reading the records, and it's wrong the moment the records change without a reprint.

beats.text: Thirteen "maybe" and 81 "definitely not". All 13 were real, so false_positive is 0. For libs/schemas, 92 were dismissed.
